messages.subject: Model comparison = anova results inconsistency?
parts:
Hi,

I have two different models, one being a model with direct effects, one being a model with mediation effects. I would like to compare these two to see which one better fits the data. Hence, I used the anova() function. However, anova (model1, model2) gives me a different result than anova(model2, model1).
Would you have an idea why this is happening? How then interpret my results?
I am just starting with SEM and Lavaan so perhaps is there a simple explanation?

Below are the two models and the associated anova results:

MODELS
------------

model1 <-'
#measurement model
PD =~ PD1 + PD2 + PD3
PR=~ PR1 + PR2 + PR3
PO =~ PO1 + PO2 + PO3
NS =~ NS1 + NS2 + NS3
JSS =~ JSS1 + JSS2 + JSS3

#Direct effect
JSS ~ d1*PO + d2*PD + d3*PR + d4*NS
'
model1.fit <- sem(model1, data=myframe.df)


model2 <-'
#measurement model
PD =~ PD1 + PD2 + PD3
PR=~ PR1 + PR2 + PR3
PO =~ PO1 + PO2 + PO3
NS =~ NS1 + NS2 + NS3
JSS =~ JSS1 + JSS2 + JSS3

#Direct effect
JSS ~ d1*PO + d2*PD + d3*PR

#Mediator effect
NS ~ ns1*PO
NS ~ ns2*PD
NS ~ ns3*PR
JSS ~ ns*NS

#Indirect effect
ns1ns:=ns1*ns
ns2ns:=ns2*ns
ns3ns:=ns3*ns

#total effect
total1:= d1 + (ns1*ns)
total2:= d2 + (ns2*ns)
total3:= d3 + (ns3*ns)
'
model2.fit <- sem(model2, data=myframe.df)

print(anova(model2.fit, model2.fit))

RESULTS:
--------------

Chi Square Difference Test

             Df    AIC    BIC  Chisq Chisq diff Df diff Pr(>Chisq)   
model1JS.fit 80 5400.2 5523.5 97.651                                 
model2JS.fit 80 5400.2 5523.5 97.651  6.126e-10       0  < 2.2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1
Chi Square Difference Test

             Df    AIC    BIC  Chisq Chisq diff Df diff Pr(>Chisq)
model2JS.fit 80 5400.2 5523.5 97.651                             
model1JS.fit 80 5400.2 5523.5 97.651 -6.126e-10       0          1


So... in one case the anova/chi sqr tells me that the mediation effects add value to the model and that the most complicated model (partial mediation, model 2) should be retained as fitting best the data (chi sqr is significant) while the second anova tells me the opposite...

Any help would be much appreciated!

Many thanks,

Nicolas

messages.author: 89c9fc822e34b78c
messages.subject: Re: Model comparison = anova results inconsistency?
parts:
> Chi Square Difference Test
>
>              Df    AIC    BIC  Chisq Chisq diff Df diff Pr(>Chisq)
> model1JS.fit 80 5400.2 5523.5 97.651
> model2JS.fit 80 5400.2 5523.5 97.651  6.126e-10       0  < 2.2e-16 ***

Note that the 'Df diff' (the difference between the degrees of freedom
of the two models) is zero. So the models have the same number of
parameters. Therefore, they can not be compared with a classic
chi-square difference test.

The 'correct' answer here would be p.value = NA (which is what you will
get in lavaan dev 0.6-1).

>              Df    AIC    BIC  Chisq Chisq diff Df diff Pr(>Chisq)
> model2JS.fit 80 5400.2 5523.5 97.651
> model1JS.fit 80 5400.2 5523.5 97.651 -6.126e-10       0          1

So, usually, anova() will automatically reorder the models according to
their degrees of freedom, but not here. Therefore you end of with a tiny
tiny negative number -6.126e-10. And it so happens that

> (1 - pchisq(-1, df = 0))
[1] 1

It should be NA again. Compare this to

> pchisq(-1, df = 0, lower.tail = TRUE)
[1] 0

and it becomes clear that the p-value is not defined if df = 0.

Yves.

messages.author: ad188126f9138663
messages.subject: Re: Model comparison = anova results inconsistency?
parts:
Nicholas,
Actually, reproducing analyses from a book sounds like a very good strategy.  However, it is hard to believe that a SEM book would give an example of attempting a chi-square difference test for non-nested models with the same df.  Perhaps something got lost in translation from the original to your code.

Ed knows the history of this better than I do, but one strategy for comparing non-nested models is the following.
(1) Construct a meta-model that includes the parameters from both models of interest.
(2) Conduct a chi-square difference test comparing each model to the meta-model.
(3) If the results differ, favor the model that does not differ in fit from the meta-model.
So, if you really do have a reason to compare such models, this offers one option.

Keith

messages.author: ad188126f9138663
messages.subject: Re: Model comparison = anova results inconsistency?
parts:
Nicolas,
   Remember that SEM is a form of analysis of covariance structure (or more generally moment structure).  You are modeling the covariance matrix, not the dependent variables.  As a result, certain concepts from generalized linear models, like the null model with just an intercept, do not carry over directly.  In SEM, the term 'null model' might instead refer to a model in which all the variables are uncorrelated.  (Moreover, by default, all variables are assumed centered in SEM, which results in zero intercepts.)  Likewise, residuals in SEM are covariance residuals, not the difference between predicted and observed values of the dependent variables.

  There are some other differences in style but not in substance between your two model syntax objects.  However, yes, the zeros are the substantive differences that fix the three effect coefficients to zero and change the df by 3.

  You can accomplish the same thing simply by omitting the corresponding variable from the right-hand-side of the line of model syntax, or omitting the entire line if you are not retaining anything on the right-hand-side.  For example, commenting out the lines would have the same effect as your fixed zeros.

# NS ~ ns1*PO
# NS ~ ns2*PD
# NS ~ ns3*PR

  You can (and this is generally a good idea) check lavaan's interpretation of your model syntax by viewing either the parameter table or the matrix representations of your model.

lavaanify(model1)
lavInspect(model1.fit, what='free')

  Just a word of caution.  Bentler & Bonett (1980) made a useful distinction between parameter nesting and covariance nesting.  If the parameters in one model form a subset of the parameters in another, as in your example, then the models are parameter nested.  Parameter nesting is sufficient but not necessary for covariance nesting.  The most famous example is that a one-factor model is covariance nested, but not parameter nested, within a model with freely estimated covariances for all pairs of variables.

Keith

Bentler, P. M., & Bonett, D. G. (1980). Significance tests and goodness-of-fit in the analysis of covariance structures. Psychological Bulletin, 88, 588-606.
